nameStory: Richardson's geranium honors Sir John Richardson, a 19th-century Scottish naturalist and Arctic explorer who documented plants across northern and western North America. Like other wild geraniums, it's also called a 'cranesbill' because its long, pointed seed pods look remarkably like the bill of a crane or stork.
description: Richardson's geranium is a hardy perennial wildflower that grows from a tough, woody taproot and spreads by underground stems called rhizomes. This mountain native reaches 8 inches to over 2 feet tall, with deeply divided palm-shaped leaves that look almost like outstretched hands. The five-petaled flowers are white to pale purple with distinctive darker purple veins that act like landing strips for pollinators.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five rounded petals, white to pale purple with prominent dark purple veins running through each petal like tiny roadmaps. Flowers are about 1/2 to 3/4 inch across with pointed green sepals beneath.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palm-shaped leaves up to 6 inches wide, deeply divided into 5 main segments that are further cut into small rounded or pointed lobes. Feel slightly rough and have a fresh, slightly peppery scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive long-beaked seed pods that look exactly like a crane's bill, with the 'beak' measuring up to 1 inch long and perfectly straight. The pods eventually split and curl to fling seeds away from the parent plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps from a deep, woody taproot that feels firm and substantial when carefully examined. Older plants spread by underground rhizomes, creating patches of connected plants.

habitat: This western mountain species is extremely rare in New England, with only one confirmed observation in the region. In its native western habitats, it thrives in mountain forests, meadows, and woodland edges from sea level to high elevations. Any New England sighting would likely be in cool, moist woodland areas or possibly escaped from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the woody rootstock, unfurling their deeply cut segments. Early spring growth has a fresh green appearance before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season, when the distinctive white to purple veined flowers are most visible and the characteristic crane's-bill seed pods begin forming.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open dramatically to disperse seeds. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the root for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the underground rootstock and rhizomes. Only the woody root system remains alive beneath the soil surface.

funFact: The crane's-bill seed pods are nature's catapults - when ripe, they split into five sections that suddenly curl upward like tiny springs, launching seeds up to 15 feet away from the parent plant with audible 'pops' that you can actually hear on quiet days!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with the much more common wild geranium, but Richardson's geranium has straighter, longer seed 'beaks' and often paler flowers with more prominent purple veining. Remember: Richardson's has a perfectly straight crane bill, while wild geranium's beak has a slight curve.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums with the common garden 'geraniums' sold at nurseries - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa! True geraniums like Richardson's are hardy perennials native to temperate regions, while garden 'geraniums' are tender plants that can't survive New England winters outdoors.
compareHints: Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments. Unlike the pink-purple blooms of wild geranium, Richardson's flowers are typically white to very pale purple, making the dark purple veins much more noticeable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
